title: Leaders Who Unintentionally Leak That They Dont Like a Team Member
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines how leaders who dislike a team member telegraph that distaste through everyday micro-behaviors, reduced eye contact, shorter replies, avoided small talk, communicating only by email, even when they believe they're concealing it. It argues the damage isn't contained to the two individuals involved; the rest of the team notices the coolness and becomes more guarded, worried about receiving similar treatment themselves. The author's prescribed fix isn't manufacturing affection the leader doesn't feel, but deliberately identifying one genuine quality in the disliked team member and focusing attention there to reduce the visible distaste. The piece frames this as a team-health issue, not just an interpersonal one, since unaddressed leakage quietly narrows open discussion across the whole group.
points: Leaders who dislike a team member almost always leak it through subtle behaviors like reduced eye contact, terse replies, and email-only communication.
The damage spreads beyond the two people involved: the rest of the team notices the coolness and becomes guarded, fearing similar treatment.
The recommended fix isn't forcing affection but deliberately identifying one genuine, respected quality in the disliked colleague to focus on.
Openness of team discussion erodes when members are quietly monitoring who is currently out of favor with the leader.
quotes: Over time, unless the leader finds their way to more connection or affinity with a disapproved team member, they will often unintentionally “leak” their dislike through their everyday behaviors.

They typically spend less time with this person, avoid communicating with them when they don’t have to, avert their attention and gaze away from them in meetings, ignore what they say during discussions, and communicate with them only through email.
Because no one knows how and why this team member fell out of favor, other team members become more cautious in their interaction with the leader.
The best way to accomplish this is to find a slice of the team member they respect, value, or appreciate.
Take the high road and find a quality of that team member you can admire.
